raw_evidence.label: Frederick Terman engineered the pipeline
raw_evidence.content: Stanford did not become a founder factory by accident. Frederick Terman (1900-1982), Dean of Engineering from 1944 and Provost from 1955, is widely called the 'father of Silicon Valley'. In the 1930s he began urging Stanford engineers to start companies near campus instead of leaving for the established East Coast electronics industry. His most famous protégés were two students named Bill Hewlett and David Packard, whom he encouraged to commercialize their work. In 1951 Terman created the Stanford Industrial Park, leasing university land to high-tech firms (Varian, HP, Kodak, GE, Lockheed) and turning the mid-Peninsula into the hotbed that became Silicon Valley. The university-to-startup pipeline this dataset measures is the direct legacy of a deliberate institutional strategy.

raw_evidence.label: Sun and Cisco were literally built on campus
raw_evidence.content: Two of the most iconic Stanford companies were born from the university's own computer infrastructure. Sun Microsystems, founded in February 1982 by Stanford grad students Scott McNealy, Andy Bechtolsheim, and Vinod Khosla (with Berkeley's Bill Joy), took its name as a pun on SUN = Stanford University Network; Bechtolsheim's founding hardware was a workstation he designed from spare parts in the Computer Science Department. Cisco Systems grew out of Stanford campus networking work in the early 1980s, its router software descended from NOS written by Stanford's William Yeager, later the basis of Cisco's IOS. These were not companies founded by Stanford alumni who happened to study there — they were spun directly out of Stanford labs.

raw_evidence.label: The landmark timeline: HP to Palantir
raw_evidence.content: The dataset contains the textbook Silicon Valley canon, datable end to end. It opens with Hewlett-Packard (1939), the original garage startup, then jumps to the 1980s wave — Silicon Graphics and Logitech (1981), Sun Microsystems (1982), Intuit (1983), Cisco (1984) — through Nvidia (1993), the dot-com duo PayPal and Google (1998), and into the social era with LinkedIn (2002) and Palantir (2003). raw_evidence.label: The tech flag is a floor, not a ceiling
raw_evidence.content: The dataset's is_tech flag is a keyword match on Wikidata's industry (P452) field — but 323 of the 545 links have no industry recorded at all. So the 104 rows flagged tech are a hard undercount: famous tech firms with a blank industry field (and there are many) are silently excluded. The analyst should treat is_tech as a lower bound and, where precision matters, identify tech companies by name rather than trusting the flag. The 'unspecified' industry bucket (323 rows) is by far the largest 'category' in the data and is an artifact of Wikidata coverage, not a real sector.

raw_evidence.content: The is_tech flag is unreliable by construction. Of 545 links, 323 (59.3%) have no industry recorded on Wikidata at all, so they can never be flagged tech regardless of what the company actually does. Only 104 links (19.1%) carry the tech flag, and another 118 have an industry that simply isn't tech. The flag is a hard lower bound — many genuine tech firms sit silently in the 323-row 'unspecified' void — and any precise tech count must identify companies by name rather than trust the flag.

raw_evidence.content: Stanford did not become a founder factory by accident. Frederick Terman (1900-1982), Dean of Engineering from 1944 and Provost from 1955, is widely called the 'father of Silicon Valley'. In the 1930s he began urging Stanford engineers to start companies near campus instead of leaving for the established East Coast electronics industry. His most famous protégés were two students named Bill Hewlett and David Packard, whom he encouraged to commercialize their work. In 1951 Terman created the Stanford Industrial Park, leasing university land to high-tech firms (Varian, HP, Kodak, GE, Lockheed) and turning the mid-Peninsula into the hotbed that became Silicon Valley. The university-to-startup pipeline this dataset measures is the direct legacy of a deliberate institutional strategy.

Frederick Terman (1900-1982), Dean of Engineering from 1944 and Provost from 1955, is widely called the 'father of Silicon Valley'. In the 1930s he began urging Stanford engineers to start companies near campus instead of leaving for the established East Coast electronics industry. His most famous protégés were two students named Bill Hewlett and David Packard, whom he encouraged to commercialize their work. In 1951 Terman created the Stanford Industrial Park, leasing university land to high-tech firms (Varian, HP, Kodak, GE, Lockheed) and turning the mid-Peninsula into the hotbed that became Silicon Valley. The university-to-startup pipeline this dataset measures is the direct legacy of a deliberate institutional strategy.
